function.name: workflow
function.description:
Run a JavaScript workflow script that orchestrates subagents at scale. Use this for work that fans out across many independent pieces — an audit over many files, a migration, multi-angle research, adversarial verification of findings — where you write the orchestration as a script instead of delegating turn by turn.

Script-body hooks:
- `agent(prompt, opts?): Promise<any>` — run one subagent to completion. Without `opts.schema` it resolves to the child's final text; with `opts.schema` (an object-rooted JSON Schema using ONLY type/properties/required/additionalProperties/items/enum/const/oneOf) it resolves to the validated object. Resolves `null` when the child fails (filter with `.filter(Boolean)`). Other opts: `label` (display), `phase` (progress group), and independent `provider`/`model` LLM target overrides.
- `pipeline(items, ...stages): Promise<any[]>` — run each item through the stages independently with NO barrier between stages (prefer this for multi-stage work). Each stage receives `(prev, item, index)`. A stage throw drops that ITEM to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- `parallel(thunks): Promise<any[]>` — run zero-argument functions concurrently and await ALL of them (a barrier; use only when a stage genuinely needs every prior result together). A throwing thunk resolves to `null`.
- `phase(title)` — start a progress phase; `log(message)` — narrate progress; `args` — the tool call's `args` input, verbatim.

Misused hooks (bad arguments, unknown options, unsupported schemas, tripped caps) end the whole script instead of producing `null`. The script has no filesystem, network, timer, or Node.js APIs; the agents do the work.

script.description: The plain JavaScript body, not TypeScript and without an `export const meta` statement; top-level await is allowed. End with `return <value>`; the JSON-serializable value is this tool's result.

meta.description: The workflow identity as plain JSON, not code.

description.description: One-line description of what the workflow does.

whenToUse.description: Optional guidance on when this workflow applies.

phases.description: Optional phase declarations matched by phase() calls.

title.description: The phase title phase() calls match by exact string.

detail.description: Optional one-line description of the phase.

provider.description: Optional provider override this phase is expected to use.

model.description: Optional model override this phase is expected to use.

args.description: Optional JSON input exposed to the script as the `args` global (wrap a bare list as a field, e.g. {"files": [...]}).

run_in_background.description: Run as a background job: return a job id immediately instead of waiting; the return value arrives with the completion notice.

{"file_path": "/home/Liangyijia_Hu/dsh-natural-workspaces/natural-dag-20261029-v001/incident/incident-report.md", "content": "# Incident Report: Checkout Outage — 2026-10-28

**Status:** Root cause identified (high confidence)
**Impact window:** 2026-10-28 09:04 UTC → ongoing at end of supplied data (09:15 UTC)
**Symptom:** Checkout p95 latency 180 ms → 4,200 ms; error rate 0.3% → 8% (edge 504s)

---

## 1. Summary

At 09:03 UTC, checkout v2.18 was rolled out with a configuration change that doubled the
per-replica database pool maximum from 12 to 24. With 6 replicas, the fleet's potential
connection demand rose from 72 to 144 — and 144 + 18 other clients = 162, which exceeds the
database's `max_connections` of 100. The database filled to its 100-slot limit within one
minute of rollout completion (09:04 UTC), and every subsequent checkout request that needed a
new connection timed out after 4,000 ms waiting in the pool queue, producing 504s at the edge.

The database itself was healthy throughout (query p95 flat at 9 ms, no lock waiters, CPU
30% → 31%); the payments service was healthy and was never even reached ("payment not called").
The edge release (v4.11) was rolled back at 09:10 UTC with no effect on the outage, ruling it
out.

---

## 2. Timestamped Causal Timeline (all times UTC, 2026-10-28)

| Time | Event | Source | Type |
|------|-------|--------|------|
| 08:58 | Edge v4.11 deployed; routing rules unchanged; adds request-id response header | `deployments.log` | Fact |
| 08:58–09:03 | Baseline steady: 100 rps, 0.3% errors, checkout p95 180 ms, db active=75, waiters=0, db CPU 30%, payments p95 28 ms | `metrics.csv`, `checkout.log`, `database.log`, `edge.log`, `payments.log` | Fact |
| 09:03 | Checkout v2.18 rollout **begins**; `database_pool_max_per_replica` changed 12 → 24 | `deployments.log`, `config/checkout-before.json` vs `config/checkout-after.json` | Fact |
| 09:03 | Metrics still at baseline (180 ms, 0.3%, active=75) — degradation not yet visible | `metrics.csv` | Fact |
| 09:04 | Checkout v2.18 rollout **complete**, replicas=6 | `deployments.log` | Fact |
| 09:04 | **Onset:** error rate 0.3% → 8%; checkout p95 180 → 4,200 ms; db active 75 → 100; db connection waiters 0 → 24 | `metrics.csv` | Fact |
| 09:04 | Database logs `FATAL remaining connection slots are reserved; active=100` (PostgreSQL-style message emitted when `max_connections` is reached and only superuser-reserved slots remain) | `database.log` | Fact |
| 09:04 | Checkout requests fail: `database connection acquisition timeout; queue_wait_ms=4000; payment not called` | `checkout.log` | Fact |
| 09:04 | Edge returns 504 at 4,200 ms for checkout upstream (4,000 ms pool-queue wait + ~200 ms overhead ≈ edge timeout) | `edge.log` | Fact |
| 09:04–09:15 | Degradation steady-state: 8% errors, 4,200 ms p95, active=100, waiters=24, FATALs continue every minute; payments remain healthy (p95 28 ms, 0 errors); db query p95 stays 9 ms, lock_waiters=0, db CPU 30% → 31% | `metrics.csv`, all logs | Fact |
| 09:10 | Edge v4.11 **rolled back**; checkout timeouts persist | `deployments.log` | Fact |
| 09:10–09:15 | No improvement after edge rollback — edge is not the cause | `deployments.log`, `metrics.csv` | Fact (observation) / Inference |

---

## 3. Root Cause (most likely, high confidence)

**The checkout v2.18 deployment oversubscribed the database connection limit.**

Arithmetic from the supplied configuration (facts):

| | `replicas` | `pool_max_per_replica` | checkout demand | `other_clients` | total demand | `database_max_connections` | headroom |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Before (`checkout-before.json`) | 6 | 12 | 72 | 18 | 90 | 100 | +10 |
| After (`checkout-after.json`) | 6 | 24 | 144 | 18 | **162** | 100 | **−62** |

Causal chain (each link supported by evidence):

1. **Config change** (fact): v2.18 raised `database_pool_max_per_replica` 12 → 24
   (`deployments.log` 09:03; before/after config files).
2. **Oversubscription** (inference, arithmetic): 6 × 24 + 18 = 162 > 100. The pool can
   never be fully satisfied; the database saturates at 100 active connections.
3. **Saturation** (fact): at 09:04, `db_active_connections` = 100 and `database.log` logs
   `FATAL remaining connection slots are reserved` — the engine refusing new connections
   because only superuser-reserved slots remain.
4. **Pool-queue timeouts** (fact): checkout requests wait 4,000 ms for a connection
   (`queue_wait_ms=4000`) and fail before doing any work (`payment not called`).
5. **User-facing 504s** (fact): the 4,000 ms wait plus overhead exceeds the edge's ~4,200 ms
   upstream timeout → `upstream_status=504 latency_ms=4200` in `edge.log`; error rate 8%.

The timing is consistent: the 09:03 metrics row (rollout in progress) is still healthy; the
09:04 row (rollout complete, all 6 replicas on the new pool size) is the first degraded row.

**Why the pool grew to 100 rather than staying at 75:** with the old cap of 12/replica the
fleet held ~72 checkout connections (75 active total incl. other clients). After the change,
each replica's pool is allowed up to 24, so pools collectively opened connections until the
database's 100 slots were exhausted; the remaining demand (24 waiters in `metrics.csv`)
queued and timed out.

---

## 4. Alternative Hypotheses (considered and ruled out)

| # | Hypothesis | Verdict | Evidence |
|---|-----------|---------|----------|
| A | **Edge v4.11 release caused the outage** | Ruled out | (1) Release notes say routing rules unchanged, only a response header added (`deployments.log` 08:58). (2) Rolled back at 09:10 with **no improvement** — timeouts persisted (`deployments.log`, `metrics.csv`). (3) The edge 504s are a *symptom* (upstream timeout), not a cause: the edge faithfully reports a 4,200 ms upstream latency that matches the checkout-side 4,000 ms pool wait. |
| B | **Database degradation** (slow queries, locks, CPU) | Ruled out | `database.log`: `query_p95_ms` flat at 9 ms, `lock_waiters=0` throughout; `metrics.csv`: `db_cpu_percent` 30 → 31%. The DB is healthy; it is *connection-exhausted*, not slow. |
| C | **Payments service degradation** | Ruled out | `payments.log`: `status=healthy p95_ms=28 errors=0` for the entire window; `checkout.log` shows `payment not called` — requests died at connection acquisition, before payments was invoked. |
| D | **Traffic spike** | Ruled out | `metrics.csv`: `requests_per_second` constant at 100 across the whole window. |
| E | **v2.18 code change introduced a slow/failing query** | Not supported | The failure occurs at *connection acquisition*, before any query runs; db `query_p95_ms` is unchanged at 9 ms. The only v2.18 change documented in the evidence is the pool-size config change. (Residual uncertainty: the supplied evidence does not include the full v2.18 diff, so an undocumented code change cannot be 100% excluded — but none is needed to explain the data.) |

---

## 5. Mitigation Plan

### Immediate (restore service)

1. **Revert the pool-size change** — the fastest, lowest-risk fix:
   - Preferred: roll back checkout to v2.17 (restores `database_pool_max_per_replica=12`), **or**
   - If a full rollback is not possible, hot-patch the config to `database_pool_max_per_replica=12` and recycle the 6 replicas.
   - Expected effect: fleet demand returns to 72 + 18 = 90 ≤ 100, restoring the +10 headroom.
2. **Do not** "fix" this by raising `database_max_connections` as the primary action: it is a
   heavier operation (in PostgreSQL it requires a database restart) and it papers over the
   misconfiguration. It may be used as a *temporary* bridge only if the rollback cannot be
   performed quickly, and must be followed by the config revert.
